title: Neba
description: The subset of the Neba component library an agent can describe: eighteen components whose every prop is a literal, an enumerated value or a reference to another component by ID.
instructions:
Neba is a React component library. Every component below is a real one, and what you write here is turned into that component rather than into markup.

## Laying a surface out

Nothing has a margin of its own. Two components sit beside each other only inside a `Flex`, and the gutter between them is that `Flex`'s `spacing`. Nest a vertical `Flex` inside a horizontal one to build a grid.

A component that takes a child takes an **ID**, never an inline definition, and a `Card` and an `Alert` take exactly one — wrap several in a `Flex` and pass that.

## Colour means something here

`color` is one of six semantic families and never a decorative choice. `success`, `warning` and `danger` say how something went; `info` is a note; `primary` is the product's own accent and `secondary` is the quiet one. Do not reach for a family because a screen needs variety, and do not use `danger` for anything but something that failed or something that destroys.

There is **one** `solid` control in a view — the action the view exists for. Everything else is `outline` or `text`.

## One ladder

`size` is the same five steps on every component, so an `md` Button, an `md` TextField and an `md` Select are the same height and line up in a row. Pick one size for a screen and stay on it; `density` is the prop for making something tighter, and it changes padding only.

## Fields carry their own words

A `TextField`, a `Select`, a `Checkbox` and the rest each draw their own label, helper line and error message. Never add a `Typography` above a field to label it, and never add one below it to show an error — put the message in the field's own `checks`.

## Text

Every string a reader sees is a `Typography`. Its `level` says what the text *is* rather than how big it should be: use `h1`…`h6` in order for real headings, and do not pick a heading level because you want larger text.

## Building a sentence out of a value

There are no operators. `formatString("Hello ${/user/name}")` is how a value is put into a sentence, and `formatNumber`, `formatCurrency`, `formatDate` and `pluralize` are how a number or a date is written in the reader's own language. Never assemble a date out of its parts.

Flex.description: The layout component. A row or a column of other components, with a gutter between them. Everything that is not one thing on its own goes inside one of these: there is no other way to place two components beside each other.

children.description: The components inside it, by ID, in the order they are laid out.

direction.description: Which way the children run. `horizontal` is a row and `vertical` is a column.

spacing.description: The gutter between the children, in steps of 0.25rem: `4` is 1rem. It is the only spacing there is — components carry no margins of their own.

justifyContent.description: How the leftover space along the direction is shared out. `space-between` pushes the first and last child to the ends.

alignItems.description: Where the children sit across the direction.

wrap.description: Lets the children fall onto another line when they do not fit. Set it on a row of chips or of cards; leave it off on a row of two buttons.

Card.description: A sheet with a heading on it. Use it to group things that belong together and to give them a name. It holds exactly one child, so put a `Flex` inside it when there is more than one thing to show.

child.description: The single component inside the card, by ID. Wrap several in a `Flex` and pass that.

title.description: The heading. A card with no title is usually a `Flex` with a border and should be one.

variant.description: The weight of the sheet. `outline` is a hairline, `solid` a filled panel, `text` no sheet at all.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

color.description: The family the edge and the focus ring take. The sheet itself is never dyed: a card holds other people's content, and tinting the paper under it puts every colour on that content on a background nobody chose.

density.description: How tightly it packs its content. Padding only — never a height and never the type scale, so a compact control still lines up with a default one beside it.

elevation.description: How far it sits off the page, as a drop shadow. `0` means no shadow at all, and is right for almost everything: the surface already has an edge. Raise it only for something that genuinely floats over the content around it.

Divider.description: A rule between two sections, with an optional word set into it. Reach for it only when the space a `Flex` already gives is not enough to separate two things.

label.description: A word set into the line — "or", "Today".

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

Typography.description: Text. Every word a reader sees goes through this: there is no other component that draws a string.

level.description: What the text *is*, not how big it should be. `h1`…`h6` are headings and are drawn as real heading elements, so use them in order and do not pick one for its size; `lead` is the opening paragraph, `caption` a note under something, `overline` a small label above a figure.

weight.description: How heavy it is. A heading is already heavier than body text, so this is for the rare line that has to stand out inside one weight.

align.description: Where the text sits in the width it has.

color.description: A semantic family, and it is deliberately not set by default: text in a paragraph is the paragraph's colour. Set it only when the colour *means* something — a figure that is over budget.

lines.description: Cuts the text off after this many lines with an ellipsis. Do not put it on anything a reader has to read.

Image.description: A picture. It reserves its space before the file arrives, so nothing on the page moves when it lands.

alt.description: What the picture says for a reader who cannot see it. Write the meaning, not the file name; an empty string is the right answer for a picture that is pure decoration.

ratio.description: The shape of the box, as width over height: `1` is a square, `1.7777` is 16:9. Give it one whenever you know it — it is what stops the page jumping when the picture loads.

fit.description: What the picture does inside that box. `cover` crops to fill it and `contain` fits the whole picture inside it.

rounded.description: Rounds the corners by one step of the radius ladder.

Chip.description: A short label on a small surface: a tag, a status, a filter that has been applied. One or two words — anything longer is `Typography`.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

color.description: The family. It is the one thing a chip says beyond its word, so let it mean something: `success` for a state that is good, `danger` for one that is not.

count.description: A number set after the label, for a chip that stands for a group.

selected.description: Draws it as chosen. For a row of filters where some are on.

Avatar.description: The mark that stands for a person or an organisation. It falls back to the initials of `name` when there is no picture, so `name` is worth giving even when `src` is.

name.description: Whose it is. It becomes the accessible name, and its initials are what is drawn when there is no picture.

shape.description: A circle for a person, a square for an organisation or a thing.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

color.description: The family behind the initials, when they are what is drawn.

Statistic.description: One figure with its name over it, and optionally how it has moved. The right component for a number a reader is meant to take in at a glance; a number inside a sentence is `Typography`.

unit.description: What it is measured in, set after the value in smaller type.

caption.description: A line under the figure — the period it covers, where it came from.

previousValue.description: What it was before. Giving it is what draws the delta; without it there is nothing to compare against.

betterWhen.description: Which direction is good news, and therefore which colour the delta takes. Set it to `down` for anything that should be falling — failures, latency, cost — or a drop will be drawn in red.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

align.description: Where the block sits in the width it has.

DataList.description: A list of label-and-value pairs: the details of one thing, in a column, with the values lined up. Use it instead of writing "Status: open" as a sentence.

items.description: The rows, in the order they are read.

orientation.description: `horizontal` puts the label beside the value, which is what a details panel wants; `vertical` puts it above, for a narrow column or for values long enough that a label beside them would leave the row mostly empty.

dividers.description: Draws a hairline between the rows.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

density.description: How tightly it packs its content. Padding only — never a height and never the type scale, so a compact control still lines up with a default one beside it.

Alert.description: A message about something that happened, set into the page it is about. Not a popup and not a toast: it sits where the thing it is about is.

child.description: The body, by ID. Usually a `Typography`.

title.description: The headline. With it the alert is a heading and the detail under it; without it the body is the whole alert.

color.description: Which kind of message it is, and the one prop here that carries meaning. `info` is a note, `success` something that went right, `warning` something to look at before it goes wrong, `danger` something that failed. The shape of the mark changes with it too, so the message is not carried by colour alone.

variant.description: The weight of the surface. `text` draws no box, which is right for an alert set among form fields.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

density.description: How tightly it packs its content. Padding only — never a height and never the type scale, so a compact control still lines up with a default one beside it.

Button.description: A control that runs something. Use it for an action, never for navigation between pages and never as a way of making text pressable.

text.description: What the button does, as a verb: "Save", "Send the invite". Not "OK".

variant.description: How loud it is. There is **one** `solid` button in a view — the thing the view is for — and everything else is `outline` or `text`. Three filled buttons in a row is three buttons with no answer.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

color.description: The family. Use `danger` for something that destroys, and leave the rest alone: a button is not coloured for variety.

density.description: How tightly it packs its content. Padding only — never a height and never the type scale, so a compact control still lines up with a default one beside it.

elevation.description: How far it sits off the page, as a drop shadow. `0` means no shadow at all, and is right for almost everything: the surface already has an edge. Raise it only for something that genuinely floats over the content around it.

loading.description: Shows a turning ring and stops the button running again. For the moment between a press and its answer.

disabled.description: Unavailable. Say why somewhere the reader can see, or a disabled button is a dead end.

fullWidth.description: Stretches it to the width it is given.

TextField.description: A field a reader types into. The label, the helper line and the error message are all part of it — do not draw any of them as separate components.

label.description: What the field is asking for. Always give one: a placeholder is not a label, because it goes away as soon as anything is typed.

placeholder.description: An example of what to type, shown while it is empty.

description.description: A helper line under the field — the format, the limit, why it is being asked.

multiline.description: Makes it a box rather than a line. For a sentence or more.

rows.description: How tall a multiline field starts.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

color.description: The family the edge, the ring and the caret take.

density.description: How tightly it packs its content. Padding only — never a height and never the type scale, so a compact control still lines up with a default one beside it.

required.description: The field has to be filled in.

readOnly.description: Shown but not editable. Different from `disabled`: the value still matters and can still be copied.

fullWidth.description: Stretches it to the width it is given.

NumberField.description: A field that holds a number, with steppers and a format. Use it rather than a `TextField` whenever the answer is a quantity: it clamps, it steps, and it writes the number in the reader's own language.

description.description: A helper line under the field.

step.description: How much a stepper moves it.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

color.description: The family the edge, the ring and the caret take.

density.description: How tightly it packs its content. Padding only — never a height and never the type scale, so a compact control still lines up with a default one beside it.

required.description: The field has to be filled in.

Checkbox.description: One yes-or-no answer, or one member of a set that can have several. Use it when the answer is submitted with a form; use a `Switch` when it takes effect the moment it is pressed.

label.description: What is being agreed to. Write it so that ticked means yes.

description.description: A helper line under the label.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

Switch.description: An on-and-off that takes effect the moment it is pressed. The difference from a `Checkbox` is time, not shape: nothing is submitted, so there is no Save to press afterwards.

label.description: What is being turned on. Write it as the thing, not as a question.

description.description: A helper line under the label.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

color.description: The family the track takes when it is on.

RadioGroup.description: A set of options where exactly one is chosen and all of them are worth reading. Past about five, use a `Select` instead — a list of fifteen radios is a list.

value.description: Which option is taken, by its `value`.

options.description: The options, in the order they are read.

description.description: A line under it, for an option that needs explaining.
A helper line under the set.

orientation.description: Which way the options run. A column is nearly always right; a row only works while every label is one word.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

color.description: The family the chosen dot takes.

Select.description: One value chosen from a list that is folded away until it is opened. Use it when there are more options than a reader wants to read, or when the choice is a detail rather than the point of the screen.

value.description: Which option is taken, by its `value`.

placeholder.description: What the trigger says while nothing is chosen.

options.description: The options, in the order they are listed.

label.description: What this option says. Left out, the value is shown.

group.description: A heading over this option and the ones next to it that name the same group. A group is a run of adjacent options, so the order of the array is the order of the list.

description.description: A helper line under the field.

variant.description: The weight of the trigger, which is a field's shell.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

color.description: The family the edge and the ring take.

density.description: How tightly it packs its content. Padding only — never a height and never the type scale, so a compact control still lines up with a default one beside it.

fullWidth.description: Stretches it to the width it is given.

Slider.description: A number chosen along a range, where roughly right is good enough and the ends mean something. When the exact figure matters, use a `NumberField`.

size.description: How big it is. One ladder for the whole library: an `md` Button, field and Chip are the same height and line up in a row.

color.description: The family the filled part of the track takes.

required.description: True when the value is not empty. The check to put on every field that has to be answered.

length.description: True when the value is between `min` and `max` characters long. Either bound may be left out.

regex.description: True when the value matches the pattern. Reach for `email` before writing one of these.

numeric.description: True when the value is a number, and between `min` and `max` if either is given.

email.description: True when the value looks like an email address.

formatString.description: Fills the `${…}` placeholders in the string with what they point at in the data model. It is the only way to build a sentence out of a value: there is no string concatenation anywhere in this catalog.

formatNumber.description: Writes a number in the reader's own language, with the digit grouping that language uses.

formatCurrency.description: Writes an amount of money, with the symbol and the placement that language uses.

currency.description: An ISO 4217 code, such as `USD` or `KRW`.

formatDate.description: Writes a date in the reader's own language. Never assemble one out of numbers: the order of the parts is exactly what differs between languages.

pluralize.description: Picks the wording that goes with a count. English has two forms and other languages have up to six, which is why this is a function rather than a ternary.

openUrl.description: Opens an address. It is an action rather than a value, and it is the renderer that decides whether a new tab is involved.

and.description: True when every one of them is.

or.description: True when any one of them is.
